newsitem.title: USA: Great Western reviews bid, suitor sees delay.
newsitem.headline: Great Western reviews bid, suitor sees delay.

text.p: Great Western Financial Corp said Tuesday it wanted to take all the time necessary to make a careful evaluation of suitor H.F. Ahmanson and Co's $6.2 billion bid while Ahmanson responded that Great Western's efforts were nothing more than delaying tactics.
Wall Street analysts and arbitragers said the rhetoric was standard boilerplate for a hostile takeover battle and in the final analysis shareholders will have a chance to make their views known.

"They're (Great Western) just insulating themselves as best as possible from Ahmanson taking a predatory position and forcing management's hand," said Todd Pitsinger, analyst at Friedman, Billings, Ramsey & Co, referring to Great Western's moves. "They want to ensure that they have the final say."
"They have done some maneuvering that presumably will buy some time," said a Wall Street arbitrager who did not want to be identified.
Specifically, Great Western said it was postponing an annual shareholders meeting that had been set for April 22. A new date for the meeting was not set.
Great Western also said it has adopted a broad severance plan for its employees in event of a change of control.
Great Western said that it will oppose a solicitation of consents of shareholders planned by Ahmanson.
Last Friday, Great Western amended its bylaws to stretch out the time required to get a shareholder vote via proxy solicitation.

After Ahmanson made a formal request last week to solicit proxies, Great Western has 10 days to announce a record date to determine which shareholders can vote. The record date must be within a maximum of 10 days of the announcement.

A spokesman for Ahmanson said the proxy solicitation would be twofold, with the first part supporting the concept of a merger and asking that steps be taken to support the Ahmanson proposal unless there is an alternative available which has better value. The second part of the solicitation would keep Great Western from granting excessive lock up fees, breakup arrangements or stock options without the approval of shareholders.

In a press release Tuesday, Ahmanson asserted that Great Western was engaging in "self serving tactics" which it said were "destructive to shareholder value and the best interests of Great Western employees.

A source close to Great Western disagreed with Ahmanson's interpretation. "The board will take its time and will carefully consider all the alternatives and will not be rushed to judgment, nor should Great Western shareholders be rushed to judgment," the source said.

Analysts believe Great Western is trying to line up a friendly bidder to rescue it from Ahmanson. "In all likelihood they are out there with their investment bankers soliciting other bids for the company," Pitsinger said.
"My expectation is that these guys are beating the bushes to come up with alternatives," said the arbitrager.

A research report Monday from Alex. Brown & Sons analyst J.K. Morford said Washington Mutual Savings Bank, often mentioned as a "white knight" rescuer for Great Western, could be "stretching itself a bit too thin" having recently completed the acquisition of American Savings. The analyst said combining Great Western and Washington Mutual "would carry a high degree of integration risk."

Pitsinger said if Great Western strikes a deal with Washington Mutual, which would in all likelihood be a stock transaction, a strong point in its favor would be that Washington Mutual has a 10-year track record of outperforming the Standard & Poor's 500 index.
Washington Mutual has said it would not comment on rumors or speculation.

Pitsinger agreed that Ahmanson, headquartered in Southern California as is Great Western, could wring more cost savings than other bidders out of a merger. But he said Seattle-based Washington Mutual could get close enough in cost savings to make a competitive bid.

Gary Gordon of PaineWebber Group Inc said in a report Tuesday that Ahmanson "would seem to have an insurmountable advantage" over any competitors in the event of a bidding war. He noted that Ahmanson could achieve the greatest cost savings.
